item.title: Afghanistan: Humanitarian Update, October 2026
item.description:
Country: Afghanistan
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Funding shortfalls threaten winter response in Afghanistan

As temperatures begin to fall across Afghanistan, humanitarian partners are ramping up winter preparedness amid significant funding constraints. Aid organizations are pre-positioning supplies to enable them to deliver assistance before access to remote communities becomes more challenging. With needs expected to remain high, the humanitarian response enters the winter season facing a substantial funding gap, raising concerns about being able to reach all those in need and forcing difficult choices about how the limited resources are prioritized.

The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan requires US$1.71 billion to provide life-saving assistance and protection across Afghanistan. However, as of October, only $550 million has been received through the Plan, meaning 68 per cent of funding requirements remain unmet. This shortfall threatens efforts to support vulnerable communities during one of the most challenging seasons of the year.

Winter often brings heightened humanitarian risks across Afghanistan. In many provinces, heavy snowfall and freezing temperatures can isolate communities, disrupt transportation routes and limit access to markets, health facilities and other essential services. For households already struggling with poverty, food insecurity, climate-related shocks and limited livelihood opportunities, the cold season brings additional pressure as families seek to secure food, heating fuel, warm clothing and adequate shelter.

As winter approaches, many vulnerable families are expected to face increasing pressure as food prices, heating costs and other seasonal expenses rise while livelihood opportunities decline. Yet several critical sectors remain significantly underfunded.

Food Security and Agriculture, the largest sector in the humanitarian response, has received only 18.2 per cent of its funding requirements despite continued concerns over food insecurity across the country. As winter conditions reduce income-generating opportunities and increase household expenditure on food, fuel and other essentials, many families are likely to face greater difficulties in meeting their basic needs.

Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items cluster, which provides vulnerable households with shelter support, essential household items and winter assistance, has received only 15.1 per cent of the funding required. Water, Sanitation and Hygiene programmes are similarly underfunded, with just 16.6 per cent of requirements met, while Nutrition activities have received 16.3 per cent. Health is funded at 45.4 per cent, leaving significant gaps in essential services, particularly as winter conditions increase the risk of respiratory infections and other seasonal illnesses.

Together, these funding shortfalls risk limiting access to food, shelter, health care, safe water and nutrition support during one of the most challenging periods of the year, potentially leaving vulnerable households with fewer options to cope.

item.title: DR Congo: Compte rendu de la réunion mensuelle du mois d'octobre 2026
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Sources: Nutrition Cluster, UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

La réunion conjointe PRONANUT-Cluster Nutrition du 27 octobre 2026 a réuni environ 60 partenaires. Les échanges ont porté sur la méthodologie de calcul des personnes dans le besoin pour le HNRP 2027, la préparation de la revue annuelle 2026 du PRONANUT, la réponse nutritionnelle à Ebola dans les CTE/CT et les interventions des partenaires.

Les discussions ont mis en évidence un faible niveau de rapportage et des besoins nutritionnels encore non couverts. Elles ont souligné la nécessité de renforcer la coordination, d’actualiser les projets dans Activity Info (HPC 2026) et de concentrer les interventions sur les zones prioritaires insuffisamment couvertes.

item.title: DR Congo: Cluster Protection RDC : Aperçu des violations et abus des droits humains dans la province du Sud-Kivu, octobre 2026
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: Protection Cluster

Please refer to the attached file.

En octobre 2026, la situation de protection au Sud-Kivu s’est considérablement détériorée, marquée par une intensification des affrontements entre groupes armés dans les territoires de Walungu, Kabare, Kalehe, Mwenga et Fizi. Cette dégradation se serait traduite par la présence d’engins explosifs dans des zones d’habitation, des actes de représailles, ainsi que des recrutements forcés, y compris d’enfants.

●Forte hausse des violations des droits : 2 466 violations ont été identifiées en octobre, soit +62% par rapport à septembre (1 524), le niveau le plus élevé depuis juin.

●Engins explosifs : Des engins explosifs auraient été lancés lors des affrontements à Kaziba, dans le territoire de Walungu, causant la mort de plusieurs civils, dont une femme et ses deux enfants, ainsi que la destruction d’une école.

●Recrutement d’enfants : 44 allégations de recrutement et d’utilisation d’enfants ont été documentées, notamment à Kalehe, Mwenga, Fizi et dans la plaine de la Ruzizi.

●Représailles : Des civils accusés de collaboration auraient été arrêtés, torturés et auraient vu leurs maisons incendiées, notamment à Itombwe (Mwenga) et à Kabare.

item.title: oPt: Gaza's Education Crisis: A System-Wide Collapse Threatening an Entire Generation
item.description:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: American Near East Refugee Aid

Please refer to the attached file.

AN ENTIRE GENERATION OUT OF SCHOOL

The war that began on October 7, 2023 did not just interrupt schooling in Gaza, it dismantled the education system that more than 750,000 learners, from preschool through university, once relied on.1 Nearly all schools have been damaged or destroyed, and for over two years, students of all ages have had little to no access to formal learning.

A child who was seven when this began is now nine or ten, and has spent a third of the life that they can remember waiting for school to resume.

This report is based on Anera's Gaza Education Sector Needs Assessment, which draws on interviews and focus group discussions with teachers, parents, students, education officials and community members across Gaza, alongside secondary data from UNRWA, UNICEF, the Education Cluster, the Palestine Central Bureau of Statistics and other humanitarian and education partners.

What emerges is a story of systemic collapse in education, one that has stripped away not just classrooms, but the routines, relationships and sense of future that schooling once provided. The war's psychological toll is equally profound. Children have endured repeated familial displacement, loss and violence, while teachers are coping with their own trauma even as they try to support students.

Yet, despite overwhelming challenges, Gaza's communities continue to demonstrate remarkable tenacity. Parents, volunteers and educators have created informal classrooms and learning activities wherever possible, underscoring the determination to keep young people learning and the urgent need for sustained international support. Children cannot recover academically without first having stability, routine and protection. Restoring education in Gaza should therefore begin with three essentials: safe places to learn, teachers who are supported and able to teach, and basic classroom resources.

This report tells the story of what has been lost and lays out what must happen next.

item.title: 2025 Annual Report: Libya: Division Entrenches Violations and Undermines Accountability [EN/AR]
item.description:
Country: Libya
Source: Libya Crimes Watch

Please refer to the attached files.

Libya Crimes Watch Issues Its 2025 Annual Report

London, 8 April 2026 — Libya Crimes Watch (LCW) has published its 2025 Annual Report, entitled “LIBYA: DIVISION ENTRENCHES VIOLATIONS AND UNDERMINES ACCOUNTABILITY“, documenting the continued and escalating grave human rights violations and international crimes occurring across the country, against a backdrop of the absence of effective accountability pathways and the persistence of impunity.

The report records 859 grave violations documented during 2025, compared to 589 during 2024, reflecting a significant increase in the rate of violations. It draws primarily on 93 documentation files and direct testimonies from victims, survivors, and witnesses collected by LCW’s field team in accordance with LCW’s established documentation methodology, which is aligned with international protocols for the documentation of human rights violations. These violations affected 617 civilians and occurred across at least 29 major areas and cities in eastern, southern, and western Libya, including remote and hard-to-reach areas.

The report provides a legal analysis of the documented violations in light of IHRL and IHL, drawing on indicators that measure the gravity, patterns, and scale of violations, and concludes that certain of these violations may constitute international crimes by virtue of their systematic nature and scale.

The Annual Report highlights the continuation of serious patterns of violations, including arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance, torture and ill-treatment, extrajudicial killing, and the denial of basic fair trial guarantees, alongside trafficking in persons, forced labour, and sexual violence. It further documents the repeated targeting of human rights defenders, activists, journalists, and dissidents for exercising their fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and participation in public life.

The report addresses violations committed against migrants, asylum seekers, and refugees, as well as vulnerable and marginalised groups, including women, children, and religious, ethnic, and gender minorities, and highlights the various contexts in which these violations occurred, including casualties resulting from military operations, encompassing armed clashes and the explosion of ERW.

The 2025 Annual Report identifies the responsibility of the authorities in eastern and western Libya for these violations, as well as that of prominent commanders and officials, whether for their commission by affiliated or supporting security apparatuses and armed groups, or for their failure to fulfil legal obligations to prevent violations, protect civilians, investigate incidents, and ensure the accountability of perpetrators. The report further highlights the continued inability of the national justice system to conduct independent and effective investigations, and the persistent weakness of cooperation with international justice mechanisms, including the ICC.

Commenting on the report, Ali Omar, Executive Director of Libya Crimes Watch, stated:

“Every year we find ourselves confronted with the same patterns of violations recurring, whilst victims and their families continue to await justice. This reality reflects an ongoing failure by the Libyan authorities to halt violations and hold those responsible to account, and underscores the urgent need for serious action to bring an end to impunity.”

In its recommendations, LCW affirms the urgent need to take concrete steps to end grave violations and international crimes, ensure the accountability of those responsible, and end impunity, including through full cooperation with the ICC. It calls upon the authorities in eastern and western Libya to honour their legal obligations, guarantee the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms, and cease the targeting of civilians on account of their opinions or activities. It further urges the international community to support justice and accountability pathways and to cease any direct or indirect support to parties implicated in violations.

For enquiries or interview requests, please get in touch with LCW Communications and Outreach Officer Nour Khalifa at Nour@lcw.ngo.

Follow us on social media: @LCWNGO.

Description

The report, “The Cost of EU-Libya Cooperation on Migration: Serious Human Rights Violations against Migrants, Refugees and Asylum Seekers,” is a joint analytical report by the International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) and Libya Crimes Watch (LCW).It documents patterns of serious human rights violations against migrants in Libya and provides a multidimensional analysis of the role of European migration management policies in perpetuating and exacerbating these violations. The report also presents a set of recommendations addressed to Libya, the European Union and its Member States, focusing on ending violations against migrants in Libya and ensuring the protection of their rights.

item.title: At least 64 children killed and 64 injured in Yemen as intensified hostilities approach three-month mark
item.description:
Country: Yemen
Source: UN Children's Fund

NEW YORK, 18 November 2026 – At least 64 children have been killed and 64 injured in Yemen since hostilities escalated on 3 September. The number of casualties is likely to increase as renewed fighting continues around densely populated areas, particularly in Taiz and Lahj.

“The rising number of children killed and injured in Yemen is devastating. It must stop,” said UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russell. “Behind every number is a child whose life has been cut short or changed forever.”

Basic services and infrastructure children depend on are also being directly impacted. At least seven schools and 28 health facilities, including five supported by UNICEF, have been damaged since the escalation began. On 2 November, an attack on the UNICEF-supported Al-Suqyah Health Centre in Lahj, which serves around 1,700 people, was reported to have killed five people, including three health workers.

At the same time, displacement is accelerating. More than 330,000 people, including an estimated 174,000 children, have been displaced since the beginning of the renewed military escalations. Many displaced families are sheltering in unfinished or damaged buildings and struggling to access food, safe water, and health care.

The situation in Taiz City is particularly alarming. With the main road from Aden closed and alternative routes insecure, more than 800,000 people have reportedly been cut off from humanitarian assistance as of late October. Water production has fallen by nearly 50 per cent, food and fuel prices have more than doubled, and shortages of medicines, fuel, medical oxygen and electricity are threatening emergency, maternal, and newborn care.

Across escalation-impacted areas, over 1,160 schools have closed or suspended learning, affecting more than half a million students. Meanwhile, around one in three children recently screened by UNICEF mobile health teams were found to be acutely malnourished. Overcrowded displacement sites, too few latrines, and limited access to safe water are also increasing the risk of disease.

UNICEF is expanding its emergency response to reach up to 350,000 people, redeploying health and nutrition mobile teams to displacement sites and affected communities in Aden, Lahj, Abyan, Marib and Taiz, scaling up emergency water and sanitation support, and providing psychosocial care and case management for children, including those who are unaccompanied or separated from their families.

“Yemen’s children have suffered so much. We urgently need safe and unimpeded humanitarian access,” said Russell. “All parties must comply with their obligations under international law. Children must be protected, including their access to essential services such as healthcare, education, safe water, and food.”

item.title: World: Community-led negotiations
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Centre of Competence on Humanitarian Negotiation

Please refer to the attached file.

The Centre for Competence on Humanitarian Negotiation (CCHN) commissioned the Humanitarian Policy Group at ODI Global to conduct research on community-led negotiations, particularly the processes that community negotiators undertake to engage with authorities and armed actors for
humanitarian access and protection.

Specifically, the study seeks to answer the following research questions:

  • What triggers the decision to engage in direct negotiations?
  • How do community negotiators prepare for such engagements?
  • What is the process taken in negotiations?
  • What are their risk-mitigation strategies?
  • What are the tactics and strategies used in the negotiation process?
  • What factors influence the outcome of negotiations?
  • What follow-up actions take place once an agreement is reached?
  • What type of support do community negotiators most need?

The findings presented in this report identified that community negotiation practices are often instinctual, unstructured, and rarely documented. Stemming from 13 countries across diverse contexts, the results strongly suggest that community negotiators prepare strategically for dialogue, similarly to what is set out in the Naivasha Grid. As noted, the greater the international support, the more aligned the community negotiations become with international humanitarian practices. However, the process varies according to the context and is generally more organic than international negotiation practices.

item.title: World: Protection negotiations with armed actors
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Centre of Competence on Humanitarian Negotiation

Please refer to the attached file.

Recent years have seen a growing recognition of the need to strengthen negotiations for protection outcomes. Yet, there is a gap in evidence and analysis on the triggers that lead to protection negotiations, the processes and practices used, and the outcomes achieved.

The Centre for Competence on Humanitarian Negotiation (CCHN) gathered insights from its global network of humanitarian professionals and commissioned the Humanitarian Policy Group at ODI Global to conduct further research on existing protection negotiation practices.

Specifically, this research seeks to address the following questions:

  1. How are protection negotiations defined and operationalised?
  2. What are the best practices in protection negotiations, and how do they vary?
  3. What contributes to or undermines successful negotiations, and what lessons can be learned?
  4. What are the patterns of protection negotiation outcomes?
  5. What are the barriers to strengthening protection negotiations as standard practice? What
    could enable it?

The findings presented in this report identify concrete negotiation practices to advance protection outcomes.

item.title: HCR TCHAD | Rapport opérationnel hebdomadaire du 15 novembre 2026
item.description:
Countries: Chad, Sudan
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Réponse d’urgence à l’Est

L’afflux continu de réfugiés soudanais en quête de sécurité au Tchad accentue la pression sur les capacités d’accueil, particulièrement à Tiné, où le centre de transit accueille désormais plus de 9 000 réfugiés, soit neuf fois sa capacité initiale. Entre le 1er et le 15 novembre 2026, 5 411 nouveaux réfugiés soudanais ont été enregistrés dans les provinces du Ouaddaï, du Wadi Fira et de l’Ennedi Est, portant à plus de 989, 827 le nombre total de nouveaux arrivants accueillis au Tchad depuis le début du conflit au Soudan en avril 2023. Ces nouvelles arrivées sont principalement liées à la persistance des violences et de l’insécurité au Darfour, ainsi qu’aux attaques contre les infrastructures civiles. Conformément à sa tradition d’asile et au principe de non-refoulement, le Gouvernement tchadien a continué de garantir l’accès au territoire aux personnes fuyant le conflit au Soudan et à la protection internationale. Le HCR et ses partenaires ont poursuivi les activités d’enregistrement, de suivi de protection, de relocalisation et d’assistance vitale, avec une attention particulière portée aux personnes les plus vulnérables. Bien que le rythme des arrivées reste inférieur aux pics précédemment observés, notamment en septembre, la poursuite des mouvements transfrontaliers continue d’exercer une pression importante sur les capacités d’accueil, les services de protection et, plus largement, la réponse humanitaire dans l’est du Tchad. La relocalisation des réfugiés soudanais vers des sites plus sûrs se poursuit. Entre le 1er et le 15 novembre, le HCR et la CNARR ont relocalisé 2 170 réfugiés soudanais depuis la zone frontalière d’Adré vers Metché, dans le Ouaddaï, leur permettant ainsi d’accéder à de meilleures conditions de protection et aux services essentiels. Au 15 novembre 2026, 154 370 réfugiés restaient en attente de relocalisation dans les zones frontalières, notamment à Adré et à Tiné. La poursuite des opérations de relocalisation demeure essentielle pour réduire la pression sur des capacités d’accueil fortement sollicitées, offrir aux réfugiés des conditions plus sûres et améliorer leur accès à la protection et à l’assistance humanitaire. Mise en œuvre progressive de l’Approche basée sur la vulnérabilité et les capacités dans les sites de réfugiés de l’Est du Tchad. Entre le 26 et le 31 octobre 2026, le HCR et ses partenaires ont poursuivi la mise en œuvre de l’Approche basée sur la vulnérabilité et les capacités (ABVC) dans les sites accueillant des réfugiés dans l’est du Tchad. Au total, 48 025 ménages réfugiés à Aboutengué, Metché, Zabout, Djabal, Goz-Amir et Kerfi ont reçu les résultats de leur évaluation. Ces résultats permettront au HCR et à ses partenaires de mieux cibler et prioriser l’assistance en fonction des vulnérabilités et capacités identifiées, tout en renforçant le suivi des ménages ayant des besoins spécifiques. La communication des résultats et le mécanisme de gestion des réclamations se sont poursuivis à Metché, Milé et Touloum, tandis que les préparatifs ont été finalisés à Amdjarass en vue du déploiement de l’ABVC à Ouré Cassoni à partir du 3 novembre. Entre le 2 et le 8 novembre, le HCR et ses partenaires ont facilité le départ de 21 réfugiés soudanais de l’est du Tchad vers le Canada. Douze réfugiés ont bénéficié d’un programme de la réinstallation, deux d’une reunification familiale et sept personnes reinstallés au Canada par les voies complémentaires. Le HCR poursuit ses efforts en faveur des solutions durables dans l’est du Tchad, notamment à travers l’accompagnement des réfugiés et le traitement des dossiers de réinstallation et de regroupement familial.

item.title: History of UNHCR in Türkiye 1960 to 2026
item.description:
Country: Türkiye
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

UNHCR has been present in Türkiye for more than six decades. Its presence was formally endorsed in 1960, marking the beginning of a long-standing partnership with the Government and people of Türkiye. In April 1962, Türkiye ratified the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, becoming its 34th State party. Türkiye subsequently ratified the 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees in 1968. In June 1967, UN High Commissioner for Refugees Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan made an official visit to Türkiye. He was received by President Cevdet Sunay and Prime Minister Süleyman Demirel. During his visit, the High Commissioner opened a refugee housing project in Istanbul, largely financed by UNHCR. At that time, UNHCR reportedly supported several projects that helped 1,400 refugees in Türkiye. Over the decades, UNHCR and Türkiye have responded to a series of humanitarian crises as refugees and asylum-seekers arrived from Iran in 1979, Iraq in 1988, Bosnia in 1993, Kosovo* in 1999, and finally Syria in 2011. Each crisis prompted significant scale-up of UNHCR’s operations. Until the early 1980s, UNHCR’s work in Türkiye largely focused on refugees from Eastern Europe. That changed between August 1982 and November 1984, when the Turkish Government, with support of the Red Crescent and UNHCR resettled around 4,000 Afghan refugees of Turkic origin from Pakistan to Türkiye. They were Kirghiz, Kazakh, Uzbek, Turkman and Uighur families, who had found temporary asylum in Pakistan, before being resettled to the east and south-east of Türkiye. In 1985, UNHCR started conducting its mandated Refugee Status Determination (RSD) in Türkiye. During the 1991 Gulf War, Türkiye faced one of the largest and fastest refugee movements. Around 500,000 Iraqis gathered in mountainous areas along the border. UNHCR provided tents in the Habur Hajj camp in Silopi. UN High Commissioner for Refugees Madam Sadako Ogata visited Türkiye to support the humanitarian response. In 2011, as thousands of refugees and asylum seekers arrived from Syria, Türkiye introduced temporary protection for all Syrians seeking safety in the country. UNHCR was invited to contribute to the development of Türkiye's new asylum legislation. To support the most vulnerable refugees, UNHCR provided tents, blankets and bed mats through the Turkish Red Crescent Society. Initially intended for newly arrived Syrians in Hatay, these supplies were also distributed to communities affected by the earthquake in Van. In 2011 alone, UNHCR provided 4,000 tents, 50,000 blankets and 10,000 bed mats.

item.title: UNICEF fast facts: World leaders meet in Manila to end violence against children
item.description:
Country: World
Source: UN Children's Fund

MANILA/NEW YORK, 18 November 2026 – As government ministers, partners, survivors, and young people gather in Manila, Philippines, for the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children this week (18 – 19th November), UNICEF is calling on governments to turn commitments made in Bogotá two years ago into sustained investment in the solutions proven to keep children safe.

“Violence against children is not inevitable. We know what works to prevent it, and we have seen what is possible when governments invest in protecting children,” said UNICEF Deputy Executive Director Ted Chaiban. “But commitments alone will not keep children safe. We need sustained investment in strong child protection systems, support for parents and caregivers, and safe schools and communities. The true measure of our progress will be whether every child can grow up free from violence, wherever they live.”

According to the latest available global data:

  • 1.6 billion children (2 in 3) experience violent discipline (physical punishment, psychological aggression, or both) by parents or other caregivers at home, including 1 in 8 who experience severe physical punishment.

  • Around 650 million girls and women (1 in 5) and around 410 – 530 million boys and men (around 1 in 7) alive today experienced sexual violence as children. This includes more than 370 million girls and women (1 in 8) and between 240 and 310 million boys and men (around 1 in 11) who experienced rape or sexual assault.

  • In fragile settings, the risk for girls is even greater, with slightly more than 1 in 4 experiencing rape or sexual assault in childhood.

  • Around 610 million children (1 in 4) live with mothers who experienced intimate partner violence in the past year.

  • In a single year, around 20 million children aged 12 to 17 (almost 1 in 5) across 21 countries experienced technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse.

    • Nearly 60 per cent of these cases took place on social media platforms.
    • More than half (57 per cent) involved someone the child already knew: a peer, partner, friend or family member.
    • More than 40 per cent of cases were never shared with anyone, and fewer than 1 per cent were reported to the police, social workers or helplines. The most common reason for not reporting the incident was not knowing where to go or who to tell.

  • Every 4 minutes, somewhere in the world, a child is killed by an act of violence.

UNICEF works with governments around the world to protect children from violence before it starts and to support them when it happens. Since 2022, UNICEF has reached 60.2 million parents and caregivers with support to raise their children without violence and helped 19.9 million children who experienced violence across 112 countries to get the care and protection they needed. Legal bans on violent discipline that UNICEF has supported now protect more than 40 million children.

UNICEF is calling on governments to fully finance and scale up proven solutions to end violence against children, including supporting parents and caregivers to provide safe and nurturing care; creating safe and enabling schools where children can learn and thrive, and strengthening accessible, inclusive, and resilient response services for every child experiencing violence.

UNICEF, the United Nations agency for children, works to protect the rights of every child, everywhere, especially the most disadvantaged children and in the toughest places to reach. Across more than 190 countries and territories, we do whatever it takes to help children survive, thrive, and fulfil their potential.

item.description:
Country: Vanuatu
Sources: Government of Vanuatu, Pacific Community

Please refer to the attached file.

DISEASE INFORMATION

Suspected case definition: A suspected case is any person with cough illness lasting >2 weeks, with at least one of the following symptoms; fits for coughing, OR; ‘whoop’ when breathing in, OR; vomiting after coughing fits.

Confirmed case definition: A confirmed case is a person who meets at least of the following criteria: Isolatin of Bordetella pertussis bacteria from a clinical specimen; OR a positive PCR test for pertussis; OR a coughing illness in person epidemiologically link by time, person, place to a laboratory-confirmed case.

Mode of transmission: Spread from person to person through respiratory droplets produced when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Outbreak Threshold: Two epidemilogically linked cases occuring within one week.

item.title: MSF MOZAMBIQUE: Teams bring healthcare closer to communities as barriers to care persist
item.description:
Country: Mozambique
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

With just one functioning health centre serving more than 138,000 people in Macomia district, Médecins Sans Frontières / Doctors Without Borders (MSF) brings primary and specialised care closer to communities, including people living with HIV. Yet these efforts cannot replace a functioning, well-resourced health system.

For people in Macomia, seeking healthcare often means making a long, costly and sometimes dangerous journey to the district’s only functioning health facility. Upon reaching it, they may find that the medicines, tests or specialised care they need are not available.

First person testimonies available here: http://prez.ly/Odqe

Macomia district covers about 4,000 km² and is home to an estimated 138,565 people1. Before the armed conflict in Cabo Delgado started in 2017, there were seven health facilities across the district; todayonly one remains functioning. It must serve residents, returnees and thousands of families displaced by insecurity2. In this region, conflict involving Islamic State Mozambique (ISM), national and regional forces affects people’s daily lives through attacks and fear of renewed violence, kidnappings and roadblocks.

Since 2019, MSF has helped to sustain access to healthcare in Macomia, adapting our services after a major attack by ISM on the town in 2024 forced a temporary suspension of activities. Having previously run our own clinic in Macomia town, MSF shifted to providing technical support to the Ministry of Health’s health centre with emergency care, maternal and child health services, while facilitating referrals to Pemba and running mobile clinics. Serving over 30,000 people, mobile clinics provide preventive and curative primary healthcare, including consultations, paediatric and basic emergency care, maternal health support, malaria diagnosis and treatment, HIV/TB screening and referral, nutrition support, mental health care, psychosocial support and health promotion. From January to September 2026, MSF teams carried out over 24,000 outpatient consultations in mobile clinics – the equivalent of around 90 consultations per day. ​

Respiratory infections were the most common condition treated, followed by malaria, which remains a major health burden in Mozambique. Over the same period, MSF teams carried out almost 9,000 sexual and reproductive health consultations and assisted 3,130 births. We also provided more than 700 mental health consultations, reinforcing a critical service in a context where needs are high but often go undetected and unmet. With only one psychiatrist based in Pemba serving a province of 2.8 million people, specialised care and referral options remain limited.

Many factors keep health care out of reach

In Macomia, multiple barriers keep people cut off from even the most basic healthcare. ​

The first barrier is reaching care at all. Distances, insecurity on the roads and damaged or non-functioning infrastructure make access difficult or impossible for many. With few and unreliable public transport options, people have to look for private means when they are already sick or in need of urgent care. ​

In many cases, the decisive obstacle iscost. A round trip from Nacate, a populated area 16.5 km away, to Macomia health centre can cost up to 1,000 meticais (about 15 USD), an unaffordable amount in a country where 81 per cent of the population lives on less than three dollars a day3.

“For a woman in labour, for a couple, for a family with a daughter who needs care, finding that amount is not easy,” says Laura Eugénio, an MSF staff member working in sexual and reproductive health in Macomia.

Recent increases in fuel price, amounting to around 12 per cent for petrol and 45 per cent for diesel4, have made this financial pressure even worse.

Reaching the health centre does not guarantee access to care. Shortages of medicines, tests and medical supplies add another barrier to diagnosis and treatment. This is a country-wide challenge and the effects are even more acute in remote and insecure districts such as Macomia. Between July and October, essential medicines that ran out included painkillers and fever reducers, antibiotics, iron and folic acid supplements – used to treat fever and infections, support maternal health and provide preventive care. ​

Shortages of rapid tests, medical and surgical supplies limited the care that health workers could provide during routine consultations. Specialised services can also be compromised. Against a backdrop of reported shortages of HIV testing kits in 93 of Cabo Delgado’s 103 health facilities, screening coverage among pregnant women with unknown HIV status at Macomia health centre’s maternity department remained below the 95 per cent target. Consistent testing is essential to offer timely treatment that protects women’s health and helps prevent mother-to-child transmission.

Staying on HIV treatment amid violence, fear and stigma

Beyond testing, insecurity and stigma disrupt HIV prevention and treatment. Attacks by ISM and fear of renewed violence can force people to flee at short notice, making it harder to stay on medication.

“I keep my medicines and my documents somewhere easy to reach,” says Suleimani, a person living with HIV in the district. “If there is an attack while I am at home, I run to take everything with me into the bush, because I now understand how important it is not to miss my medication. But not everyone is aware of that.” ​

Stigma around HIV remains widespread, and the act of seeking care itself may expose patients to discrimination. With services concentrated in the district’s only functioning health centre, confidentiality has become harder to guarantee. Some patients worry they will be recognised when attending follow-up appointments or collecting medication. ​

“Many people stop going to pick up their medicines at Macomia health centre because they fear discrimination” explains Suleimani. “There is a door at the hospital and people know that whoever goes through it is going for HIV treatment. That exposes people.” ​

Maintaining continuity of care remains a major challenge: among patients who started HIV treatment between July 2025 and March 2026, only just over half were still receiving care six months later. To help bring patients back into care, MSF health promotion teams actively trace HIV patients considered “lost to follow up” – meaning they have not shown up to their appointments for more than 61 days. Since August, more than half of the people traced have decided to return to treatment, with MSF staff accompanying them through the first steps of the process. ​

Expanding options for care

Referral data point to a high and sustained demand for obstetric care: of the 187 referrals recorded from January to September 2026, 120 were for complicated deliveries. Nearly half of the pregnant women referred to Pemba were under 20. With only one ambulance in Macomia, each transfer to Pemba leaves no other vehicle available. In September 2026, MSF completed the construction of an operating theatre attached to Macomia health centre, designed to manage complicated pregnancies and other surgical emergencies locally, reducing risky and costly transfers and improving access to timely care for mothers and newborns. ​

Given the many barriers to accessing healthcare services, MSF mobile clinics are often the only way to receive care for people in more remote parts of the district.

“There are few options left. People stay home until they get better or until it’s too late”,says Samuel, a 64-year-old patient from Nacate.

They are also instrumental in identifying patients who need higher-level care and organising referrals and transport. ​

Mobile clinics cannot replace a well-resourced health system

In recent weeks, MSF teams have observed increased attendance at some of the mobile clinics that we run outside Macomia town, putting extra strain on services designed for more remote communities. As vital as they are, mobile clinics should not be a substitute for a functioning health system. They can help reduce some of the barriers people face, but they cannot replace a network of health facilities, reliable supply chains, infrastructure and trained staff. ​

In Cabo Delgado, where conflict remains the main driver of displacement, insecurity continues to affect every aspect of people’s lives, including seeking care. Authorities have a responsibility to protect health facilities, strengthen supply chains and ensure safe access for patients and health workers. ​

Availability of water is also a critical unmet need in many communities. Without water and adequate sanitation and hygiene services, the risk of waterborne diseases increases, placing further pressure on the few functioning health facilities. Improving these conditions in communities and facilities is essential to deliver care. ​

Donors must support sustained healthcare and humanitarian presence in districts such as Macomia, which risk becoming even more isolated as funding shrinks. Without this combination of commitment from authorities and humanitarian support, people already affected by nearly a decade of conflict will continue to remain cut off and face preventable suffering.

In Cabo Delgado province, MSF also works in Mocímboa da Praia, providing technical support to the hospital and to the three functioning health centres in the district, out of a total of eight.

item.title: World: Qatar Charity’s Information and Crisis Management Center Supports Faster Humanitarian Response [EN/AR]
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Qatar Charity

Please refer to the attached files.

As natural disasters and conflicts drive displacement and increase relief needs, Qatar Charity has established an Information and Crisis Management Center to support its humanitarian operations. Launched in June 2026, the Center is one of the organization’s major humanitarian digital transformation initiatives.

According to a report published on the Ghiras website, the Centre brings together data, advanced technology, and artificial intelligence to improve response times, strengthen planning, and make humanitarian interventions more effective in crisis- and disaster-affected areas.

According to a report on the Ghiras website, the Center reflects the organization’s commitment to using data, technology, and artificial intelligence to support humanitarian action, improve planning, and enable more timely and effective interventions in crisis- and disaster-affected regions.

Why Was the Center Established?

The Center was established in response to several rapidly evolving global challenges:

  • Increasing climate-related disasters.
  • Escalating conflicts and the displacement they cause.
  • The need for real-time information to inform decisions.
  • The importance of rapid intervention during the first hours of a crisis.
  • The growing role of technology and artificial intelligence in humanitarian action.
  • The need for stronger coordination among headquarters, field offices, and partners.

What Does the Center Aim to Achieve?

The Center pursues several strategic objectives:

  • Strengthening Qatar Charity’s preparedness for emergencies and disasters.
  • Developing an early-warning system for humanitarian crises.
  • Providing senior management and field teams with accurate data and analysis.
  • Improving the efficiency of humanitarian interventions and supporting faster responses.
  • Improving resource management and identifying humanitarian priorities.
  • Strengthening coordination among relevant stakeholders.
  • Building an institutional record of crises and lessons learned.

How Does the Center Work?

The Center uses an integrated system for monitoring, analysis, and information management. Its work includes monitoring crises and disasters around the clock, collecting and analyzing data from multiple sources, and preparing regular reports and urgent updates.

It also assesses humanitarian needs, provides interactive dashboards to support decisions, and tracks developments in affected areas. These functions support the planning and coordination of relief operations, while the documentation of experience helps preserve knowledge for future responses. Technology in the Service of Humanitarian Action
The Ghiras report identifies several technologies used by the Center: artificial intelligence and data analytics, geographic information systems (GIS), early-warning systems, digital dashboards, humanitarian information-management platforms, and tools for real-time monitoring and analysis.

Together, these tools are intended to provide a comprehensive picture of humanitarian conditions, helping decision-makers act quickly and effectively.

Supporting Operations from the First Months

Following its launch in June 2026, the Center moved quickly from its establishment phase to supporting field operations.

From late August through September 2026, it monitored severe flooding across large parts of Nepal, gathering and analyzing information on the evolving situation and the needs of affected communities. This information supported Qatar Charity’s teams in identifying priorities and directing assistance.

In September 2026, the Center also monitored the arrival of a new wave of Yemeni refugees in Djibouti following renewed conflict. Its ongoing monitoring and analysis of humanitarian conditions and urgent needs supported relief efforts, coordination, and operational decision-making.

What Sets the Center Apart?

Around-the-clock monitoring: Following humanitarian crises and disasters worldwide.

Data-informed decisions: Turning information into indicators and analysis that guide action.

Artificial intelligence: Using technology to support monitoring, analysis, and risk forecasting.

Stronger institutional coordination: Connecting field offices and departments through a unified system.

Humanitarian knowledge management: Documenting experience and lessons learned to improve future responses.

Supporting the 2026–2030 Strategy

The Center’s work aligns with Qatar Charity’s 2026–2030 Strategy, which emphasizes digital transformation, institutional innovation, and stronger organizational capabilities.

By investing in technology, data, and intelligent systems, the organization aims to develop a faster, more flexible, and more effective humanitarian response model that can adapt to a rapidly changing global landscape.

***
For more humanitarian and development reports, articles, and insights, please visit the Ghiras website.

item.title: Nigeria: NCDC Lassa Fever Situation Report Epi Week 44: 26th October – 1st November 2026
item.description:
Country: Nigeria
Source: Government of Nigeria

Please refer to the attached file.

Highlights

• In week 44, the number of new confirmed cases increased from 9 reported in epi week 43 of 2026 to 13. These were reported in Ondo, Bauchi, Edo, Taraba and Nasarawa States (Table 3).

• Cumulatively, 278 deaths have been reported with a Case Fatality Rate (CFR) of 23.4% which is higher than the CFR for the same period in 2025 (18.3%).

• In total for 2026, 26 States have recorded at least one confirmed case across 122 Local Government Areas (Figures 2 and 3).

• Eighty-seven percent (87%) of all confirmed Lassa fever cases were reported from 5 states (Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue) while thirteen percent (13%) were reported from 21 states with confirmed Lassa fever cases. Of the 87% confirmed cases, Ondo reported 37%, Bauchi 23%, Taraba 12%, Edo 10% and Benue 5%.

• The predominant age group affected is 21-30 years (Range: 1 to 93 years, Median Age: 31 years). The male-to-female ratio for confirmed cases is 1:0.9 (Figure 4).

• The number of suspected and confirmed cases increased compared to that reported for the same period in 2025.

• No new healthcare worker was affected in the reporting week 44.

• National Lassa fever multisectoral multi-partner Technical Working Group (TWG) continues supporting the coordination of activities at all levels.

item.title: Somalia: FSNWG Special Report - El Niño 2026 - 2027 Sense-Making Session Brief (16 November 2026)
item.description:
Countries: Somalia, Burundi, Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, South Sudan, Sudan, Uganda, United Republic of Tanzania
Sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Food Security and Nutrition Working Group, Intergovernmental Authority on Development, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

Background

The El Niño 2026–2027 ‘sense-making’ session on October 28th, 2026, brought together experts from the IGAD Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC), Climate Hazards Center/Famine Early Warning Systems Network (CHC/FEWS NET), International Research Institute for Climate and Society (IRI), and the United Kingdom Met Office (UK Met Office) to review the evolving El Niño event and its implications for Eastern Africa.

Given that by end of October many bimodal rainfall areas across the region had not yet experienced the widespread heavy rainfall and flooding that earlier forecasts had indicated, an important question emerged: Does the relatively subdued start to the season indicate that the forecasts were incorrect, or is the season still evolving in a manner consistent with expectations for a strong El Niño event? The session sought to address this question by examining recent observations, reviewing the latest forecasts, and assessing how previous El Niño events evolved during the October-December season. Each institution presented its assessment of current conditions, the likely evolution of the season, and the associated implications for the region. The presentations were followed by a discussion with participants to identify areas of consensus, key uncertainties, and priorities for preparedness and early action.

One of the key recommendations was to monitor updated forecasts and observations, due to the early October timing of the predictions discussed on the 28th October 2026 and the value added by forecasts from early November. Early November analyses also support evaluation of rains for all of October. This report provides a timely early-mid season assessment based on and prompted by the El Niño 2026-2027 sense-

item.title: World: IOM Cash-based Interventions: Annual Report and Case Studies 2025
item.description:
Country: World
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

In 2025, cash-based interventions (CBI) continued to provide people affected by crisis, displacement and socioeconomic vulnerability with greater choice and flexibility in meeting their needs, while also supporting recovery and longer-term resilience. IOM implemented CBI in 106 countries and territories, reaching more than 1.9 million people worldwide, including over 1.7 million people in crisis settings.

The report provides an overview of IOM’s CBI globally and showcases experiences from across six regions. The case studies demonstrate the versatility of cash in responding to immediate needs while supporting recovery, resilience and self-reliance.

Across diverse contexts, CBI was most effective when embedded within broader, people-centred approaches and combined with complementary services. Community engagement, accessible community feedback mechanisms, continuous monitoring and coordination with authorities, financial service providers and humanitarian partners strengthened accountability and responsiveness. Inclusive and gender-responsive approaches helped address barriers to safe and equitable access.

The experiences also highlight the importance of preparedness and adaptable delivery arrangements, as well as pathways linking cash assistance with livelihoods, financial inclusion and social protection. Together, these practices show how CBI can address immediate priorities while contributing to longer-term resilience and sustainable solutions.

item.title: WFP Tajikistan Country Brief, November 2026
item.description:
Country: Tajikistan
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP sponsored a high-level Government of Tajikistan delegation to China, as part of efforts to strengthen a sustainable, nationally owned school feeding programme.

• WFP and the World Bank convened a high-level meeting in Dushanbe to advance Tajikistan’s wheat flour fortification agenda, agreeing on priority actions for the 2027-2030 national roadmap.

• WFP supported disaster risk reduction awareness sessions and evacuation drills in 20 schools in Rasht and Tojikobod districts.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Tajikistan is a landlocked, mountainous country with a population of 10.27 million, growing at 2 percent yearly, the highest rate in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Half of the population is under 25 years, and a quarter resides in cities (TAJSTAT, 2020).

• According to the Tajikistan Demographic and Health Survey (TDHS) 2023, stunting among children under five declined from 26 percent in 2012 to 14 percent in 2023, while wasting decreased from 10 percent in 2012 to 6 percent by 2017 and remained at 6 percent in 2023, marking a substantial improvement on nutrition outcomes over the past decade.

• Tajikistan’s economy remains strong, with GDP growth exceeding 8 percent in 2024 and early 2025, supported by remittances, services, and industry, while inflation remains low. However, the economy remains vulnerable to external shocks, with remittances accounting for nearly half of GDP and export performance remaining weak.

• Poverty declined from 20.4 percent in 2023 to 19.8 percent in 2024, driven by economic growth and remittances. Nonetheless, rural households remain vulnerable due to limited employment opportunities and exposure to climate and economic shocks.
